case.case_title: Wijeratne v. Vijitha Perera, Sub-Inspector of Police, Polonnaruwa and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Application No. 379/93, decided on 10 January 1994

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the police actions unlawfully infringed the petitioner’s right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 14(1)(b).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the seizure of posters and threats prevented the peaceful picketing campaign, infringing his right to peaceful assembly.
case_context.respondent_argument: Respondents claimed the petitioner was warned not to create disturbances and could conduct peaceful picketing, denying arrest and detention.
key_facts: Petitioner planned a peaceful, non-violent picketing campaign during lunch break.
Police seized posters and threatened remand to prevent the protest.
The planned protest was cancelled due to fear caused by police actions.
No evidence of violence or disruption was found.
Police did not have lawful authority for search or seizure.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court interpreted Article 14(1)(b) as protecting the right to conduct peaceful assembly without unlawful interference. The police actions unlawfully obstructed the petitioner’s right to assemble peacefully.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The seizure of posters and threats effectively deterred the peaceful picketing, constituting an infringement of the right to peaceful assembly. The police had no lawful basis for their actions.
principles_established: Peaceful assembly is a fundamental right protected by the Constitution.
State authorities must not unlawfully interfere with peaceful protests.
Unlawful seizure of materials and threats to suppress assembly violate Article 14(1)(b).

outcome.holding: The court held that the petitioner’s right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 14(1)(b) was infringed by the unlawful seizure of posters and threats by the police.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Compensation awarded and directions to police issued to respect fundamental rights.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(b) was materially engaged as the case involved suppression of a planned peaceful picketing campaign, directly implicating the right to peaceful assembly.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court found that the seizure of posters and threats deterred the peaceful picketing campaign, infringing the petitioner’s right to peaceful assembly under Article 14(1)(b).
